title: Fast track: files sent as a committee report
question: How many money files skip the usual wait between committee and Board, and is dissent more common on them?
finding: 206 of the 3,419 money files that a committee recommended and the Board then voted on were sent “as a committee report” (6.0%), naming $3.33 billion in their titles. The Board’s Rules of Order (Rule 4.20, edition effective June 30, 2026) allow it as an exception: “legislation deemed by a committee to be of an urgent nature, which is heard after 9:00 a.m. Thursday may be considered by the Board” as a committee report, if the committee chair asks the Clerk that morning to put it on the printed agenda. The ordinary rule is that a meeting’s new business is what committees reported out before 9:00 a.m. on the Thursday before the Tuesday meeting. In the record these files were heard on a Thursday (123), Friday (45) or Monday (35) and voted by the Board a median 5 days later; 36 were voted the next day. Other files waited a median 6 days, and 1,185 of them 12 days or more. The share peaked at 19.5% in 2017, a year in which other files waited a median 12 days, and was 1.1% in 2026; 121 of the 206 came in June, July or December. Dissent is not clearly more common on them: 9 of 206 drew a no at the final vote (4.4%) against 109 of 3,213 (3.4%), a gap chance alone would give about 43% of the time.
how: A file counts when the last committee roll call before its final Board vote prints “as committee report” or “as a committee report” in the action (209 committee roll calls carry those words; the rest of those files have no recorded final vote or were recommended again later). The wait is the number of days from that committee roll call to the Board’s first vote on the measure (the first reading, for an ordinance). The year is the year of the committee vote. The comparison group is every other money file with a recorded committee recommendation and a recorded final vote.
limits: Sending a file as a committee report is provided for in the Board’s own rules and can be an ordinary way to meet a deadline, such as a grant that must be accepted by a date, a lease about to lapse, or the last meeting before a recess. The record does not say why a file was treated as urgent. The rules on disk are the edition effective June 30, 2026; the wording in force in earlier years is not on disk. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 1 money file (160358) whose final passage is among them is left out of the counts, and none is counted as unanimous. 104 of the final votes counted here were read from the minutes. Dollar figures are the totals named in file titles: an agreement amended twice is counted at each new total, rent and accepted grants are money coming to the City as well as money going out, and budget ordinances name no single figure, so a sum of title dollars measures what the titles name, not money spent. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
